claims.text: Corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection in Q235 steel across room- and high-temperature regimes is governed by passive-layer formation and stability.
Adding Cr, Mn, and Ni can enhance the protective passive layer on Q235 steel.
The proposed material begins as Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state.
The intervention is exposure to an aggressive salt environment at 700–900 °C.
The hypothesis is intended to apply across both room- and high-temperature regimes.
Passive-layer formation and stability are the structural mediator of corrosion protection.
The thermodynamic stability of corrosion products governs corrosion behavior in aggressive salts.
Sluggish diffusion contributes to the proposed corrosion-protection mechanism.
Alloyed Q235 steel is predicted to show improved corrosion resistance and reduced mass change.
The reference material is Q235 steel without the proposed alloying additions.
The individual roles and interactions of Cr, Mn, and Ni in corrosion resistance are not fully understood.
A controlled comparison of Q235 steel with and without alloying additions under aggressive salt exposure can test the hypothesis.
Corrosion rate, mass change, and passive-layer thickness are the proposed response variables.
Failure of the alloyed material to achieve at least a 10% reduction in both corrosion rate and mass change relative to the reference would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims applicability across room- and high-temperature regimes, but the stated boundary and experiment cover only 700–900 °C, leaving the room-temperature regime untested.

The intervention field identifies salt exposure as the intervention, whereas the causal comparison in the hypothesis and experiment is alloying versus no alloying; the manipulated cause is therefore inconsistently specified.
